Android Auto 18.2 Starts Rolling Out With a Big Navigation Change for Wide Screens
13 photos
Photo: Bogdan Popa/autoevolution/Google
How about that? An Android Auto feature that actually includes a front-facing change. The all-new Android Auto version 18.2 , which is now rolling out through the Google Play Store, includes a navigation change that makes it easier to interact with apps on an infotainment unit with a wide screen.
At the moment, the Android Auto interface shows the navigation buttons at the top of the screen. This means that you must tap these buttons to interact with your apps, such as Spotify and YouTube Music, and access certain features like the music library or the recently-played tunes.
Doing this from the driver’s seat isn’t exactly the most convenient thing to do, especially on a device with a wide screen, as you must have to lean to your right specifically to be able to tap the option that is farther from you.
That’s why Google is changing this in Android Auto 18.2 by moving the navigation bar to the left, therefore bringing all options closer to the driver.
Google is tweaking the entire Android Auto UI - and the apps running on top of it - to use the screen estate more effectively. While the navigation bar is now displayed in a vertical position on the left of the screen, the music artwork and the rest of the details, including the name of the songs, are now displayed across the entire UI. The thumbnails are larger, and in so many ways, this approach makes perfect sense because all your information is much easier to read.
There’s also a mini-player that remains on top of everything else on the screen, so you can control the music playback directly from this menu, without having to open the entire Now Playing interface.
The new UI has also been updated by the dialer in the Phone app. Instead of dedicated options to access favorites, recents, contacts, and the dial pad at the top of the screen, you can now just tap these options in the vertical sidebar that appears when you launch the app.
The same approach should soon make its way to all apps on Android Auto, though for now, they appear to be limited to media apps and the dialer. Only devices with wide resolutions are getting the new navigation app, though there’s no doubt they would come in handy on all units, as the essential options would be easier to reach from the driver’s seat.
Photo: AndroidAuthority Google appears to be fine-tuning the Android Auto interface at a time when the company is also giving the finishing touches to the major update it promised in the spring. Codenamed Cielo, this update will include massive changes, beginning with new features and ending with new app categories finally being unlocked for Android Auto users.
The new update will include support for widgets, something users have been drooling after for several years already. Widgets will be displayed side-by-side with the rest of the Android Auto interface - unlike CarPlay, where widgets are shown on a separate screen - so you will be able to see the weather forecast, the next calendar appointments, and other data directly on the screen, without having to launch the full apps.
Photo: Mishaal Rahman on X The other big feature that will be part of this release is support for video apps. While methods to watch YouTube and play other media from apps not officially available on Android Auto have existed for a long time, Google is now unlocking the support for YouTube and other similar apps officially.
Users will be able to watch YouTube when their cars are stationary directly on their infotainment screens. When they begin driving, and Android Auto detects this, the application restricts the video playback for safety reasons. YouTube will allow an audio-only mode for users who pay for YouTube Premium, so they will be able to continue the playback in the background only by listening to the audio track.
All the other apps that will be able to play video on Android Auto will have to specifically integrate this audio-only mode to be able to continue the playback when the vehicle starts moving.
Browsers will also come to Android Auto. When this feature goes live, users will be able to browse the Internet directly from their infotainment screens, so they won’t need their phones anymore. Obviously, this feature will also be available only when their vehicles are parked, as the browsing won’t be allowed while driving. No further specifics have been shared, but Google Chrome and Vivaldi, the two browsers already available on Android Automotive, are very likely to get support for Android Auto.
Google hasn’t shared any ETA specifics as to when these new features should start rolling out, but there’s a good chance they would start appearing for beta users by the end of the year. Everybody else will get the same capabilities in the first quarter of the next year.
